rationale: A wins because it gives the founder more truly different sell paths and names the proof that would kill each one before it wastes a reporter's time. Its strongest line, "Who holds the keys: what customer-managed encryption actually protects against," turns a feature into a security-architecture story; B's weaker "Notion bets regulated finance and healthcare buyers will pay for control, not features" imports buyer motive the update does not prove. A still gets loose with "spent a decade dismissing," but B leaves more of the set in generic enterprise-trend fog.
gaps_in_A: "A cloud-native workspace is rebuilding for the offline case it spent a decade dismissing" invents Notion's prior dismissal and makes a historical claim the update does not support.
"Notion against Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace" imports a competitive fight not in the supplied facts; the angle asks for proof, but it still leads with the unsupported frame.
"The bank that wouldn't let its staff use Notion is now piloting it" turns an aggregate pilot claim into a specific buyer narrative; no bank, prior ban, or staff-use blocker is supplied.
"sovereignty as an upsell is standard practice" may be true, but it is not in the update. The pricing angle needs competitor pricing before it deserves to be pitched.
gaps_in_B: "Notion bets regulated finance and healthcare buyers will pay for control, not features" invents buyer motivation and sits awkwardly beside the no-pricing-change fact.
"after it added customer-held encryption keys" implies the bank pilots followed from CMEK, but the update does not say the pilots depend on the launch.
"cleared the hardest security review in the market" overstates what a pilot proves. A pilot is not a deployment or full security approval.
"compliance teams tighten on where data lives" has no current regulatory peg in the facts. The set admits the why-now is weak, which means this belongs on watch, not in the main launch push.
